stem: What is a limiting factor?

options.content: A scarce resource that restricts output
options.rationale: Correct: for example labour hours or a key material.

options.content: A cost that cannot be reduced by management
options.rationale: A limiting factor is a resource, not a cost that is fixed.

options.content: The highest price customers will pay for a product
options.rationale: That is a market limit on price, not a resource shortage.

options.content: A fixed cost that is the same at every output
options.rationale: Limiting factors concern resources, not cost behaviour.

explanation: A limiting factor is any scarce resource (labour, materials, machine time) that stops the business making all it could sell.

stem: A business with spare capacity is deciding whether to accept a special order. Which cost should be ignored?

options.content: A share of the existing factory rent
options.rationale: Correct: the rent is paid whether or not the order is accepted.

options.content: Extra materials that are needed for this order only
options.rationale: This is a relevant cost: it arises only if the order is accepted.

options.content: Overtime that would be paid only because of the order
options.rationale: This is a relevant cost caused by the decision.

options.content: Special packaging that is bought just for this order
options.rationale: This is a relevant cost of the order.

explanation: Relevant costs change with the decision. An apportioned share of existing rent does not, so it is ignored.

stem: When labour hours are the limiting factor, how should products be ranked?

options.content: By contribution per unit of product
options.rationale: This ignores the amount of the scarce resource used by each product.

options.content: By selling price per unit
options.rationale: Price alone does not show profitability per scarce hour.

options.content: By total fixed cost of each product
options.rationale: Fixed costs are not used to rank products.

options.content: By contribution per labour hour
options.rationale: Correct: the scarce resource is the labour hour.

explanation: With a single limiting factor, rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource and make the highest-ranked first.

stem: A candle maker normally sells at US\$12 with a variable cost of US\$7. It has spare capacity. A shop offers US\$9 each for 600 candles, which need extra delivery costing US\$240. What is the gain from accepting?

options.rationale: This leaves out the extra delivery cost.
This uses the normal price instead of the offer price.
The delivery cost has been added instead of deducted.

explanation: Contribution = (9 - 7) × 600 = 1,200; less extra delivery 240 = US\$960.
hints: Only variable and extra costs count.

stem: A product line has a contribution of US\$8,000 and avoidable fixed costs of US\$9,500. After apportioned fixed costs it shows a loss of US\$14,000. What is the effect of closing the line?

options.content: Profit rises by US\$14,000
options.rationale: The loss includes apportioned costs that continue after closure.

options.content: Profit rises by US\$1,500
options.rationale: Correct: avoidable costs saved exceed the contribution lost by 1,500.

options.content: Profit falls by US\$8,000
options.rationale: This ignores the avoidable fixed costs saved.

options.content: Profit is unchanged
options.rationale: The contribution lost and the costs saved are different amounts.

explanation: Closing loses contribution of 8,000 but saves avoidable fixed costs of 9,500, so profit rises by 1,500. Apportioned costs that continue do not matter.
hints: Compare the contribution lost with the avoidable costs saved.

stem: Making a component is cheaper than buying it. Which non-financial factor could still justify buying?

options.content: The component is cheaper to make in the workshop
options.rationale: That is the financial case for making it.

options.content: Making it uses the existing fixed costs of the workshop
options.rationale: That is a financial point and suggests making it.

options.content: The freed workers could earn more elsewhere
options.rationale: Correct: the freed capacity may earn more.

options.content: The cost of buying the component is higher
options.rationale: That is also a financial point.

explanation: Non-financial factors include supplier reliability, quality and the alternative use of the freed capacity and labour.
hints: Think about reliability, quality and the use of capacity.

stem: A manager refuses a one-off order because its price is below full absorption cost, although the business has spare capacity. What is the best criticism of this decision?

options.content: The manager should always accept every order that is offered
options.rationale: A price below variable cost would reduce profit.

options.content: Fixed costs continue anyway, so a price above variable cost adds to profit
options.rationale: Correct: the manager has used the wrong measure.

options.content: The manager should have used the apportioned fixed cost in the analysis
options.rationale: Apportioned fixed cost is irrelevant.

options.content: The order was refused for a non-financial reason only
options.rationale: The reason given was a financial one.

explanation: The decision should compare the price with the extra costs only. Fixed costs are incurred anyway, so a price above the variable cost adds to profit.
hints: Which costs change if the order is accepted?

stem: A department that shows a loss after apportioned fixed costs should always be closed.
explanation: False. Compare its contribution with the avoidable fixed costs; if contribution is higher, it adds to profit and should be kept.

stem: In a make-or-buy decision, an avoidable fixed cost of making is a relevant cost.
explanation: True. If the fixed cost would stop when the item is bought, it is saved by buying and is therefore relevant.
hints: Would the cost stop if the item were bought?

stem: Match each decision to the key comparison.

right.content: Price against extra variable and extra fixed costs
Variable plus avoidable fixed cost of making against the purchase price
Contribution lost against avoidable fixed costs saved
Contribution per unit of the scarce resource

explanation: Each decision compares only the relevant revenues and costs that differ between the options.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: In a decision, {{blank:a}} costs, which have already been spent, are ignored. A fixed cost that would stop if a product were closed is an {{blank:b}} fixed cost.

explanation: Sunk costs are ignored; avoidable fixed costs are relevant.

stem: Name the resource-based ranking measure used when one input is scarce: contribution per unit of the ______ .
explanation: Contribution per unit of the limiting factor (scarce resource).

stem: A uniform maker has spare capacity. Variable cost is US\$18 a uniform. A school offers US\$21 each for 900 uniforms and the order needs extra delivery of US\$450. Calculate the gain from accepting the order.
explanation: (21 - 18) × 900 = 2,700; less 450 = US\$2,250. Using a full cost that includes fixed overhead would wrongly show a loss.
workedSolution: 1. (21 - 18) × 900 = 2,700; less 450 = US\$2,250. Using a full cost that includes fixed overhead would wrongly show a loss.
hints: Contribution of the order less the extra cost.

stem: A bakery makes 2,400 boxes a year at a variable cost of US\$6 a box. Making them also needs a supervisor costing US\$3,000 a year that could be avoided if the boxes were bought. Calculate the relevant cost of making the boxes.
explanation: 2,400 × 6 = 14,400; plus 3,000 avoidable fixed cost = US\$17,400. Leaving out the avoidable fixed cost gives US\$14,400.
workedSolution: 1. 2,400 × 6 = 14,400; plus 3,000 avoidable fixed cost = US\$17,400. Leaving out the avoidable fixed cost gives US\$14,400.

stem: A supplier offers the boxes at US\$8 each. By how much is it cheaper to make the boxes than to buy them?
explanation: Buying costs 2,400 × 8 = 19,200. Making costs 17,400. Saving from making = US\$1,800.
workedSolution: 1. Buying costs 2,400 × 8 = 19,200. Making costs 17,400. Saving from making = US\$1,800.

stem: Machine time is the limiting factor. Product Y has a contribution of US\$14 a unit and uses 2 machine hours a unit. Calculate its contribution per machine hour.
explanation: 14 ÷ 2 = US\$7 per machine hour.
hints: Divide the contribution by the hours used.

stem: A workshop has 1,040 machine hours. Products have: X contribution US\$18, 3 hours a unit, demand 180 units; Y contribution US\$14, 2 hours a unit, demand 240 units; Z contribution US\$9, 1 hour a unit, demand 320 units. Calculate the maximum total contribution.
explanation: Z: 320 units use 320 hours (US\$2,880); Y: 240 units use 480 hours (US\$3,360); 240 hours remain for X: 80 units (US\$1,440). Total = US\$7,680.
workedSolution: 1. Z: 320 units use 320 hours (US\$2,880); Y: 240 units use 480 hours (US\$3,360); 240 hours remain for X: 80 units (US\$1,440). Total = US\$7,680.
hints: Rank by contribution per hour: Z, Y, then X.
Use the hours left for X.

stem: State three non-financial factors that should be considered before accepting a special order at a low price.

points.description: The effect on regular customers who may demand the same lower price
Whether there is genuine spare capacity and no loss of normal sales
The effect on staff morale, quality and the reputation of the business

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Regular customers may demand the same price; the business must have spare capacity; and quality and staff morale may be affected.

explanation: One mark for each factor.

stem: Explain why a department showing a loss may still be worth keeping.

points.description: A department's loss includes apportioned fixed costs that continue after closure
Its contribution still helps to cover those costs
Closing it loses the contribution but saves only the avoidable fixed costs, so profit may fall

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The loss includes shared fixed costs that would continue if it closed. Its contribution still helps to cover them, so closing it loses contribution and may reduce profit.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: Which costs would stop if the department closed?

stem: A manager decides to produce only the product with the highest contribution per unit, although labour hours are scarce. Evaluate this decision.

points.description: The scarce resource is labour hours, so contribution per labour hour is the right measure
The product with the highest contribution per unit may use many hours and give a lower contribution per hour
Total contribution is then lower than if products were ranked per hour
Demand limits for each product must also be respected
Judgement: the plan should be revised to rank by contribution per hour, with non-financial factors such as customer contracts considered

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: With labour hours scarce, products should be ranked by contribution per hour, not per unit. The highest contribution per unit may use many hours and give less in total. The plan should be revised, respecting demand limits and contracts.

explanation: One mark for each of the five points.

stem:
Masvingo Bags makes leather bags. The normal price is US\$22, the variable cost US\$13 and the full cost US\$17 (including fixed overhead absorbed). The workshop has spare capacity of 1,500 bags. A shop offers US\$16 a bag for 1,200 bags; the order needs extra delivery costing US\$700 and a design licence costing US\$350.

The workshop also makes 4,000 zip fasteners a year at a variable cost of US\$1 each. Making them needs tooling costing US\$1,200 a year that would be avoided if they were bought. A supplier offers them at US\$1.45 each.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the gain from accepting the shop's order.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which cost is ignored in the decision on the order?

options.content: The delivery cost of US\$700 for the order
options.rationale: This is relevant: it arises only if the order is accepted.

options.content: The design licence costing US\$350 for the order
options.rationale: This is relevant: it arises only if the order is accepted.

options.content: The variable cost of US\$13 a bag for the order
options.rationale: This is relevant: it is caused by making the extra bags.

options.content: The fixed overhead of US\$4 a bag
options.rationale: Correct: it is incurred whether or not the order is accepted.

parts.explanation: Fixed overhead absorbed does not change with the order.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Advise whether the order should be accepted, giving one assumption and one non-financial factor.

points.description: The order adds US\$2,550 to profit on relevant costs
Fixed overhead is incurred anyway, so the full cost is not the test
Assumption: the spare capacity of 1,500 bags is genuine and no normal sales are lost
Non-financial: other customers may demand the lower price, or goodwill with the shop

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Accept: the order adds US\$2,550 because the price exceeds the variable and extra costs. The assumption is that spare capacity exists. The business should watch for regular customers demanding the same price.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the relevant cost of making the zip fasteners.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Advise whether to make or buy the zip fasteners.

points.description: Making costs US\$5,200 against US\$5,800 to buy, a saving of US\$600
Recommend making them
Non-financial: buy if the supplier is reliable and the freed workers earn more elsewhere; or keep quality control in the workshop

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Making is cheaper by US\$600 (5,200 against 5,800), so continue to make the zips. Quality control and the alternative use of the workers should be considered.

explanation: This item tests a special order and a make-or-buy decision with advice.
hints: Full cost includes fixed overhead that does not change.
Include avoidable fixed costs in the cost of making.

stem:
Bulawayo Enamelware has 1,000 machine hours available each month. The three products it makes are:

| Product | Contribution per unit US\$ | Machine hours per unit | Maximum monthly demand (units) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| P | 24 | 4 | 150 |
| Q | 20 | 2 | 260 |
| R | 11 | 1 | 280 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the contribution per machine hour of:

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: After making the full demand for R and Q, calculate the number of units of P that can be made with the hours left.
parts.explanation: R uses 280 hours and Q 520 hours; 1,000 - 800 = 200 hours; 200 ÷ 4 = 50 units of P.
parts.workedSolution: 1. R uses 280 hours and Q 520 hours; 1,000 - 800 = 200 hours; 200 ÷ 4 = 50 units of P.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why ranking the products by contribution per unit would give a lower total contribution.

points.description: P has the highest contribution per unit but earns only US\$6 per machine hour
Machine time is scarce, so the contribution per hour is what matters
Making P first would use up the hours that R and Q use more profitably

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: P earns the most per unit but only US\$6 an hour. Since hours are scarce, products earning more per hour should come first.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The owner is asked to supply 100 extra units of P to a regular customer, which would reduce the production of Q. Advise, using figures and non-financial factors.

points.description: 100 units of P use 400 hours, which would replace 200 units of Q
That would lose 200 × 20 = 4,000 of contribution and gain only 100 × 24 = 2,400
On contribution alone the extra P reduces profit by 1,600
Non-financial: the customer is a regular one and goodwill may justify the loss, or other capacity could be hired

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The 400 hours for 100 units of P would replace 200 units of Q. The business would gain 2,400 but lose 4,000, a net loss of 1,600. It should accept only if goodwill with the regular customer or extra capacity makes up for it.

hints: Compare the contribution gained with the contribution lost.

explanation: This item tests limiting factor ranking, a plan and an evaluation of a change.
hints: Rank by contribution per machine hour.
